## Why This Matters

Every lesson so far reported one number — accuracy for classifiers, R-squared for
regressions — and moved on. That single number can hide a model that is quietly
useless.

Imagine screening for a disease that afflicts 9% of a population. A "model" that
declares *everyone healthy* is correct 91% of the time. 91% accuracy — and it
catches **zero** sick patients. The accuracy is real and the model is worthless,
because accuracy rewards the majority class and says nothing about the errors that
cost the most. This lesson builds the metrics that tell the truth — and the paired
lab puts them to work on a real screen, spotting a rare disease in coqui frogs.

::: {.callout-tip title="Analogy"}
A smoke detector that **never goes off** is right almost every day — fires are rare.
But "right almost every day" is exactly the wrong thing to measure; you want to know
*did it catch the fire?* (recall) and *when it shrieked, was there really a fire?*
(precision). Accuracy is the useless daily score; precision and recall are the two
questions that actually matter.
:::

## The Confusion Matrix

Every classification metric is computed from one small table that cross-tabulates
what the model said against the truth. For a positive class (say, "sick"):

| | Predicted positive | Predicted negative |
|--|--------------------|--------------------|
| **Actually positive** | True Positive (TP) | False Negative (FN) — a *miss* |
| **Actually negative** | False Positive (FP) — a *false alarm* | True Negative (TN) |

The two diagonal cells are correct; the two off-diagonal cells are the two *kinds*
of error, and they usually cost very different amounts. Accuracy collapses all four
into one ratio, $\frac{TP+TN}{\text{all}}$, which is why it can look high while the
FN cell — the misses — quietly fills up.

## Precision and Recall

Two ratios read straight off the matrix, each answering one of the smoke-detector
questions:

$$\text{Precision} = \frac{TP}{TP + FP} \qquad \text{Recall} = \frac{TP}{TP + FN}$$

- **Precision** — of everything the model *flagged positive*, what fraction really
  was? It punishes **false alarms**. Maximize it when a false positive is expensive:
  a spam filter that dumps a real email, a fraud block on a legitimate card.
- **Recall** (also *sensitivity* or *true positive rate*) — of all the *actual
  positives*, what fraction did the model *catch*? It punishes **misses**. Maximize
  it when a false negative is dangerous: a disease screen, a fault detector.

They pull against each other: flag more aggressively and you catch more positives
(recall up) but raise false alarms (precision down). The **F1-score** packages the
trade into one number — the *harmonic* mean, which stays low unless *both* are
decent:

$$F_1 = 2 \cdot \frac{\text{Precision} \cdot \text{Recall}}{\text{Precision} + \text{Recall}}$$

In the lab, a logistic model scores **accuracy 0.943** on the disease screen — yet
its **recall is only 0.346**: it misses two-thirds of the sick. Accuracy hid that;
recall exposed it.

## The Threshold Is a Dial

A classifier like logistic regression does not emit a label — it emits a
*probability* (`predict_proba`, from L04). The 0.5 cutoff that turns that score into
a label is just a **default**, and you are free to move it. Lower the threshold and
the model flags more cases: recall rises, precision falls. Raise it and the reverse.
The threshold is an **operating point** you choose for the cost structure — there is
no universally right value.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
  Q["Scoring a classifier"] --> B{"Balanced classes,<br/>FP and FN equally costly?"}
  B -->|yes| ACC["Accuracy is fine"]
  B -->|no| C{"Which error hurts more?"}
  C -->|"a miss (FN)"| REC["Lower the threshold;<br/>watch recall and F1"]
  C -->|"a false alarm (FP)"| PRE["Raise the threshold;<br/>watch precision"]
  C -->|"want one threshold-free score"| AUCN["Report ROC-AUC"]
```

## ROC and AUC

If the threshold is a dial, why report just one operating point? The **ROC curve**
sweeps *every* threshold and plots the **true positive rate** (recall) against the
**false positive rate**, $FPR = \frac{FP}{FP + TN}$ — the fraction of healthy
patients wrongly flagged. A model that ranks positives above negatives hugs the
top-left corner; a coin-flip rides the diagonal.

The **AUC** (Area Under the Curve) collapses that whole curve into one number:

- **AUC = 1.0** — perfect ranking; **0.5** — no better than chance.
- It is **threshold-independent** — it measures whether the model's *scores*
  separate the classes, before you commit to any cutoff. The lab's model scores
  AUC **0.889**.

AUC is the right summary when you want a single threshold-free comparison — but on
*heavily* imbalanced data it can look flatteringly high (the huge TN count keeps FPR
small), so precision-recall curves are the honest companion (named, not drilled
here).

## Regression Metrics

Regression has no confusion matrix; you measure how far predictions miss:

| Metric | Formula idea | Reads as |
|--------|--------------|----------|
| **MSE** | mean of squared errors | average squared miss; punishes big errors hard (L03's loss) |
| **RMSE** | square root of MSE | same **units as the target** — the headline error size |
| **MAE** | mean of absolute errors | typical miss; robust to outliers |
| **R-squared** | 1 - (model error / baseline error) | share of variance explained; 1.0 perfect, 0 = predict-the-mean (L03) |

RMSE is the usual headline (interpretable units); MAE when outliers shouldn't
dominate; R-squared for a unit-free "how much better than the mean" (the baseline
from L03).

## Common Pitfalls

- **Quoting accuracy on imbalanced data.** The headline sin of this lesson — the lab
  runs the all-healthy baseline at 0.913 to make it concrete.
- **Reporting precision without recall (or vice versa).** Either alone is gameable:
  flag nothing for perfect-looking precision; flag everything for perfect recall.
  Report the pair, or F1.
- **Reading metrics on the training set.** Metrics are a held-out measurement (L09);
  training-set precision/recall flatter exactly like training accuracy did.
- **Trusting AUC blindly under heavy imbalance.** A high AUC can still hide poor
  precision at every usable threshold — check the operating point you will actually
  ship.

::: {.callout-note title="Deep Dive: why F1 is a harmonic mean (Optional)" collapse="true"}

The harmonic mean of precision $p$ and recall $r$ is $2pr/(p+r)$. Unlike the
ordinary average, it is dragged toward the *smaller* of the two: a model with
precision 1.0 and recall 0.02 has arithmetic mean 0.51 but F1 $\approx 0.039$ — the
harmonic mean refuses to be fooled by one strong number when the other is near zero.
That is exactly the behavior you want from a single "are *both* decent?" score. The
**F-beta** generalization, $F_\beta = (1+\beta^2)\frac{pr}{\beta^2 p + r}$, tilts the
balance: $\beta > 1$ weights recall more (use when misses are costlier), $\beta < 1$
weights precision more.
:::

## FAQ / Industry Reality

**"Which single metric should I report?"** — Name the costs first. If a miss is
worse than a false alarm (disease, fraud, faults), lead with recall (or F-beta with
beta > 1); if a false alarm is worse (spam, blocking good transactions), lead with
precision; if you must compare models before fixing a threshold, report AUC; if
classes are balanced and the two errors cost the same, accuracy is genuinely fine.

**"So accuracy is useless?"** — No — it is the right metric for *balanced* problems
with *symmetric* costs (the coqui calls from earlier lessons were roughly balanced,
so accuracy served honestly there). It only lies when the classes are skewed or the
errors cost differently — which, in the real world, is most of the time.

**"My data is 99% negative and AUC is 0.95 — am I done?"** — Be careful. AUC can stay
high while precision at every usable threshold is poor, because the enormous TN count
keeps FPR tiny. Look at precision and recall at the threshold you would actually
deploy, and consider a precision-recall curve.

## Summary / Cheat-sheet

| Concept | The one-liner |
|---------|---------------|
| Accuracy trap | high accuracy can hide a useless model on imbalanced data |
| Confusion matrix | TP / FP / FN / TN — every classification metric starts here |
| Precision | TP/(TP+FP); of those flagged, how many right; punishes false alarms |
| Recall | TP/(TP+FN); of actual positives, how many caught; punishes misses |
| F1 | harmonic mean of precision and recall; both must be decent |
| Threshold | the dial that trades recall for precision (an operating point) |
| ROC-AUC | TPR vs FPR across thresholds; 1.0 perfect, 0.5 chance; threshold-free |
| Regression | RMSE (units of target), MAE (outlier-robust), R-squared (vs mean) |
| Pick by cost | choose the metric that matches the cost of FP vs FN |
